items.risk: Results remain exposed to agricultural commodity spreads, energy prices, policy incentives and mark-to-market timing.
Policy incentives and favorable energy/corn economics contributed to ethanol performance, limiting confidence in straight-line extrapolation.

Successor bottleneck can migrate from processing capacity to feedstock availability, logistics, policy credits or end-market blend economics; additional crush capacity does not guarantee durable margin capture.
Substitution by alternative feedstocks, competing crush capacity or non-crop low-carbon fuels can weaken the renewable-fuel demand channel even while food/feed infrastructure remains useful.
Margin and earnings sensitivity to policy, commodity spreads, energy prices and mark-to-market timing can create confidence inflation if a favorable quarter is annualized without normalization.
Capacity additions can invite industry supply response; if crush capacity grows faster than renewable-oil/feed demand, utilization may rise while unit margins compress.
Prior segment-disclosure control weakness raises the value of independent filing-level reconciliation when Alpha constructs numeric score evidence.
A substantial portion of liquidity is committed credit capacity rather than cash on hand; availability does not itself establish future operating profitability or commodity-cycle resilience.
The carbon-removal credits are not yet certified or issued; market demand, realized pricing, audit outcome and economic contribution remain unproven.

contradictions.contradiction: Strong segment profit growth includes meaningful favorable timing/mark-to-market effects and policy-sensitive economics.

Q2 network utilization and segment profit demonstrate operating leverage, but approximately $100M of favorable mark-to-market/timing effects and policy-supported biofuel economics mean headline profit cannot be treated as pure structural improvement.
